source_title: Anduril Awarded $99.6M for U.S. Army Next Generation Command and Control Prototype
angle: The Anduril story is no longer just a $99.6 million Army prototype. In 15 months, the Army has moved NGC2 from an OTA experiment to a common battlefield data layer led by Anduril, with Palantir and Raft inside the architecture, a separate $20 billion Anduril enterprise contract in the background, and a new Anduril-announced award worth $162.8 million initially and up to $1.8 billion over five years. The accountability story is whether “continuous competition” is becoming a single-vendor battlefield integration spine before public oversight can catch up.
selection_reason: This has the clearest live accountability angle: a major defense-tech company claims a $99.6M Army OTA award to build a next-generation command-and-control prototype with Palantir, Microsoft and others, raising investigable questions about procurement oversight, vendor selection, battlefield software accountability, data integration and who bears operational risk. Unlike the podcast-history items, this is current, documentable through federal records and Army sources, and well suited to Marta’s focus on decision chains and institutional responsibility.
article:
**The Army’s Anduril prototype has become a battlefield software gatekeeping test**

The important number in the Anduril-Army command-and-control story is no longer $99.6 million.

That was the figure in July 2025, when the U.S. Army said it would use an Other Transaction Authority agreement to have “Team Anduril” deliver a Next Generation Command and Control prototype to the 4th Infantry Division. The award was real: the Army described it as an 11-month, $99.6 million OTA for an integrated suite of command-and-control capabilities across hardware, software and applications, built around a common data layer. ([army.mil](https://www.army.mil/article/287180))

The newer figure is larger, and more consequential. On October 5, 2026, Anduril said the Army had awarded it a contract to expand delivery of the NGC2 common data layer beginning with I Corps, with a $162.8 million base period and options that could bring the total to $1.8 billion over five years. ([anduril.com](https://www.anduril.com/news/anduril-continues-to-scale-next-generation-command-and-control-across-the-army?utm_source=openai)) As of publication, Machina Daily found Anduril’s announcement and trade-press reporting of the award, but not a matching Army release with the same October 2026 contract value.

That distinction matters. The public story began as a prototype. The emerging story is about who controls the software and data layer through which battlefield systems are supposed to connect.

NGC2 is the Army’s attempt to replace siloed command systems with a “technology stack” that includes transport, infrastructure, data and applications. The Army says the system is not a single product, but an ecosystem intended to help commanders make faster decisions by integrating data from previously separate warfighting systems and enabling AI and machine-learning tools to organize and analyze that data. ([army.mil](https://www.army.mil/article/287180))

The official procurement narrative is competition. After the July 2025 Anduril OTA, the Army awarded a separate $26 million OTA to a Lockheed Martin team for division-level prototyping with the 25th Infantry Division. It said more than 80 vendors submitted proposals during the NGC2 Commercial Solutions Opening and described flexible vendor teams, continuous onboarding and “continuous competition.” ([army.mil](https://www.army.mil/article-amp/288233/army_announces_additional_competitive_award_for_next_generation_command_and_control_ngc2_prototyping_efforts))

But the record since then shows a narrowing decision. In June 2026, the Army announced that it had established the NGC2 common data layer baseline. Anduril would lead it. Palantir would remain partnered with Anduril to provide an edge-to-cloud data mesh using Anduril’s Lattice and Palantir’s Foundry, with Raft providing data and services registries, transformation tools and data federation. ([army.mil](https://www.army.mil/article/293409/army_and_industry_align_on_common_data_baseline_as_next_generation_command_and_control_moves_from_prototyping_to_delivery))

That is the accountability hinge. If NGC2 becomes the Army’s operational command-and-control architecture, the “data layer” is not a neutral accessory. It determines how sensors, fires systems, vehicles, applications and commanders’ screens exchange information. The company leading that layer gains influence not only over its own software, but over the terms on which other vendors’ tools must integrate.

The Army is aware of the lock-in problem. Its releases emphasize modularity, open architectures and vendor teaming. A September 2026 Army article described a “Right to Integrate” strategy, saying the Army had pushed vendors to expose APIs and use modular open systems so disparate radars, sensors and effectors could merge into a common operating picture. That same Army article named Anduril’s Lattice as an AI-enabled integration tool and said divisional-scale exercises with the 4th Infantry Division had shown the architecture could be operated and expanded by soldiers in the field. ([army.mil](https://www.army.mil/article/295204/accelerating_multi_domain_interoperability_through_open_software_architectures))

The unresolved question is how open that openness remains once the Army begins buying at scale.

The March 2026 Anduril enterprise contract makes the issue sharper. The Army said it had awarded Anduril a 10-year enterprise contract to consolidate procurement of the company’s commercially available technologies, replacing more than 120 separate procurement actions with a single framework. The contract has a five-year base period, a five-year option period and an estimated value of up to $20 billion. ([army.mil](https://www.army.mil/article/291074?utm_source=openai))

That does not mean Anduril has received $20 billion. It means the Army created a very large contracting vehicle through which future orders can flow. But it also means that, when the Army decided in June that Anduril would lead the NGC2 common data baseline, there was already a broad Anduril buying channel in place.

Other Transaction Authority is designed for speed and flexibility, especially for prototypes. It is also designed to sit outside many normal procurement rules. The Government Accountability Office has repeatedly warned that OTAs require stronger data and oversight. In a 2025 report, GAO said OTAs can reduce cost oversight risk protections and that improved contracting data would help the Defense Department assess whether these agreements are effective. ([files.gao.gov](https://files.gao.gov/reports/GAO-25-107546/index.html?utm_source=openai)) Earlier GAO work on Army modernization found inconsistent practices for collecting and sharing lessons learned from alternative agreements. ([gao.gov](https://www.gao.gov/products/gao-21-8?utm_source=openai))

None of that proves wrongdoing in the Anduril awards. It does show why the decision chain deserves scrutiny.

The Army’s argument is urgency. It has said NGC2 validation was informed by months of field events with the 4th and 25th Infantry Divisions. In May 2026, according to the Army, 4th Infantry Division’s Ivy Mass exercise stressed NGC2 at division scale across Fort Carson and Piñon Canyon, including cyber and electromagnetic attacks. The 25th Infantry Division tested integration across Hawaii, the continental United States and the Philippines during Balikatan 2026. ([army.mil](https://www.army.mil/article/293409/army_and_industry_align_on_common_data_baseline_as_next_generation_command_and_control_moves_from_prototyping_to_delivery))

The operational case is plausible. Ukraine has shown how fast data, drones, fires and electronic warfare can compress decision cycles. A battlefield command system that cannot ingest new sensors or survive degraded communications is a liability.

But speed does not answer ownership.

The Army’s budget documents show NGC2 is also becoming a programmatic funding structure, not just a set of experiments. For FY2027, Army budget materials identify Program Element 0605331A for C2 Applications, describing it as part of a new funding structure for NGC2 application-layer investment, with a $488.4 million request for the program element. ([hitchintel.com](https://hitchintel.com/programs/0605331A?utm_source=openai)) That shift matters because funding lines create constituencies, schedules and expectations. Once a software architecture becomes the basis of budget planning, the cost of changing course rises.

Anduril’s own October announcement says “no single company should control every element” of the Army’s command-and-control stack. ([anduril.com](https://www.anduril.com/news/anduril-continues-to-scale-next-generation-command-and-control-across-the-army?utm_source=openai)) That is the right principle. The test is whether the Army’s contracting structure enforces it.

Several questions remain unanswered in the public record.

What technical rights does the Army have to the interfaces, schemas, registries and deployment tools that make the NGC2 data layer work? If Anduril, Palantir or Raft is replaced, can the Army continue operating the baseline without degraded capability or emergency sole-source work? Who decides whether another vendor’s application is truly interoperable? What happens when fielded AI-enabled tools produce a wrong operating picture: is responsibility assigned to the application vendor, the data layer, the integrator, the unit commander or the acquisition office that accepted the risk?

The Army has named many participants. It has not yet made the accountability map equally visible.

The real story, then, is not that a defense-tech company won a prototype. It is that the prototype appears to have helped define the layer on which future battlefield software will depend. The Army may be solving an urgent operational problem. It may also be concentrating technical leverage faster than its public oversight mechanisms can explain.
